articles.title: Parish churches need support to preserve the tradition of choral evensong
articles.summary: Letter: Dr Andrew James Sillett of St Giles’ church in Oxford says parish churches need help to flourish just as cathedrals do
body: Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins (Letters, 13 October) is right to highlight the severe financial pressures facing England’s cathedrals and the threat that this poses to choral music. Yet the future of choral evensong depends not just on cathedrals. Across the country, there are parish churches that sustain choirs, train young organists and offer regular opportunities for children and adults to participate in this living tradition.

I am a churchwarden and singer at St Giles’ church in Oxford, where locally recruited choirs of boys, girls and teenagers sing choral evensong every Sunday. Alongside these choirs, around 40 organ students are currently learning through the church, and we are investing in a major new pipe organ to support future generations of musicians.

Parish churches often face many of the same financial pressures as cathedrals, but with fewer resources and less professional support. However, they remain uniquely placed to recruit locally and adapt quickly to changing circumstances.

At St Giles’ church, we are developing new ways of widening access to choral and organ education that should prove just as important to the future of the tradition as preserving historic institutions themselves.

If we focus only on preserving cathedrals, we risk overlooking the wider musical ecosystem that sustains English choral evensong. This tradition will flourish only if both cathedral and parish churches are enabled to pass it on to future generations.Dr Andrew James SillettChurchwarden, St Giles’ church, Oxford

articles.title: Why are French police so violent? Their job is to protect the state, not the people
articles.summary: Officers are instruments of state whose job is to repress, rather than manage, public dissent
body: Familiar images of teargas clouds drifting across Paris squares, police baton charges against masked protesters and terrified teenagers floored – and worse – by stun grenades have once again focused the world’s attention on France’s policing methods.

While most of its western European neighbours generally favour police tactics that prioritise crowd containment and de-escalation, France has long responded to social movements that take to the streets with, at times, shocking physical force.

The reasons why are a complex mix of history, politics, state organisation and a particular security culture that has become deeply ingrained over decades, if not centuries, and whose limits continue to be pushed today.

French policing policy is rooted in Napoleon’s ultra-centralised state and in the political philosophy of the Republic. In France, the police are an instrument of the state. Their core task is to protect it, enforce its laws, and maintain public order.

Conceptually, that is a far cry from, for example, the UK, where since the early 1800s the police have been considered servants of the public, whose authority derives from public consent and whose chief responsibility is to keep the peace.

French police officers are agents of state authority. That means protests, blockades and mass disorder are not just civil nuisances, but direct challenges to the authority of the republic. The police’s priority is to reclaim the streets, not to negotiate.

That explains the aggressive tactics, such as systematically encircling and trapping crowds, and their continued use of “intermediate” or less-than-lethal weapons, many of which are banned or heavily restricted elsewhere in Europe.

Defence ball launchers, for example, fire rubber projectiles at 185mph (300kph). The explosive grenades that injured gilets jaunes protesters in the late 2010s and killed an environmental protester in 2014 have been phased out, but been replaced by pyrotechnic stun grenades.

Designed to disperse crowds through both impact and a 160dB acoustic shock, these have caused multiple injuries in recent years, including lost eyes and teeth, fractured jaws and several amputated limbs. They also frequently instil mass panic.

Violent policing methods are also fostered by France’s almost unique culture of street protest. A legacy of insurrection dating back to the 1789 revolution means protesters know the street can, and generally does, force governments to back down.

Unlike in Germany or the Netherlands, French unions, while they may strike often, are not formal government negotiating partners. The top-heavy, presidential structure of the Fifth Republic marginalises institutional consultation.

That means a heavily centralised state often passes laws with little popular agreement, making the “power of the street” one of citizens’ few viable means of forcing concessions. Protest here is regarded as a civic duty and a legitimate democratic tool.

That creates a vicious circle. French authorities see large crowds as an existential threat, so send in the police. Their military-style tactics entrench the aggression and alienate peaceful demonstrators. This prompts the more radical groups to opt for more violent tactics. But rather than isolating those elements, police respond with baton charges and munitions. And that turns protests into battles.

Data from conflict monitoring organisations, such as Acled, consistently shows that France, perhaps surprisingly, does not always record western Europe’s highest number of demonstrations (Germany and Italy also vie for that title).

But it does show that France consistently records the highest rates of escalated, high-intensity unrest, including street barricades, widespread vandalism and looting, arson attacks and direct confrontations between protesters and police.

France’s approach to policing and crowd management has for decades drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors and civil society groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Council of Europe.

Reports have documented instances of excessive force, misuse of grenades and rubber bullets, arbitrary mass arrests and routine teargas deployment against largely non-violent protesters. But the model persists, and is even expanding.

Last month, thousands marched in protest at a proposed “licence to kill” law seeking to establish a legal “presumption of self-defence” for police officers and gendarmes using firearms in the line of duty.

The law, opposed by civil rights groups, leftwing politicians, the magistrates’ union and the UN, would in effect shift the burden of proof on to victims and their families to demonstrate that a police shooting was disproportionate.

In essence, critics argue, it would institutionalise police impunity; reinforcing, once more, a security culture that treats public dissent and social tension not as democratic realities to be managed, but as insurrections to be repressed. The battle for France’s streets is far from over.

articles.title: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject plan to leave Canada in referendum
articles.summary: Result is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity
body: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin the process of independence, delivering a decisive victory for supporters of Canadian unity and deepening divisions within the separatist movement.
With nearly 1.9m votes counted, roughly 76% people supported remaining in Canada, while 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, Alberta’s capital, celebrated the result.
“Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.
The results showed an overwhelming majority of Albertans had voted to remain and one radio show host posted: “Someone owes Albertans $130m for this theatrical waste of taxpayers’ money.”
Pollster David Coletto told the Guardian that residents felt the referendum was “a distraction away” from what they wanted their government to focus on.

“There was almost a general sadness about the wasted energy spent on this rather than the more real threats they see, including the Trump administration,” he said. “Most Albertans feel deep grievances with the federal government while also being proudly Canadian. The marriage may be rocky at times, and most Albertans want to see some thing changed, but very few are willing to see the marriage end.”

The province’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

Others took a different view of the results. “The result is bleak. Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat, however, it changes nothing about the reality of the circumstances Albertans find themselves in,” David Parker, a longtime far-right organiser linked to a massive breach of voter information, wrote on social media.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.
Related: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.

Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.

Smith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a by-election.

Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence. And in the aftermath of the results, one prominent separatist leader said he would push for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith.

Jeffrey Rath told Global News that the Alberta independence will remain nothing but a dream long as Smith, whom he called an “avowed federalist” remains in power. He said it was time for separatists to “take back ownership” of the UCP.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.

“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff
articles.summary: Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it
body: To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.

But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.
Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.
Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.
John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokingly described himself as a “musician (and a hunk)”.
The Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabet introduced himself to his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.
Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.
Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse, posted a photograph of herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.

Prominent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha, whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, who identified as a political scientist and astrophysicist.

All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.
Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.

“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.
“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.

Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also has well-documented ties to members of Rio’s mafia underworld and once employed the relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trump recently designated a foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonaro voiced surprise at those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.
On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.
Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.

The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.

Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwinger won the 4 October first round by more than 2m votes.

articles.title: Fleeing the frontline: Yemeni families cross Red Sea to Djibouti as Houthi conflict rages
articles.summary: Their overland routes to safety blocked off, several thousand people have boarded boats to escape gunfire, bombing and a dire humanitarian situation
body: Abubaker Saeed was fishing in the Red Sea off Yemen’s coast last month when he noticed explosions in the distance. His mind turned immediately to his wife and two children, and he raced back to his home village of al-Wahijah.

Aircraft from the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemeni government forces had launched airstrikes in surrounding areas, targeting members of the Iran-aligned Houthi militia as its fighters approached the nearby port city of Mocha.
“They were bombing Houthis while Houthis were 1km away from us,” the 50-year-old recalled.

By the time he reached the shore, the rebels had arrived and were battling government forces on the ground. As Saeed tried to get to his house, he witnessed three people being shot and killed in the fighting.
He managed to make it through the havoc of bombings and shootings to reunite with his family in his house, where they hid as the fighting raged for 12 hours until the government forces withdrew.

When the fighting ended, Saeed decided it was no longer safe for his wife and children – aged nine months and five years – to stay in al-Wahijah. Because Houthis had taken control of all the overland routes to safer areas of Yemen, he had no option but to try to take his family across the Bab al-Mandab strait to Djibouti. They headed to the shore, about 1km from their house, carrying nothing but the clothes on their backs.
They boarded a boat with about 80 other people. The operators charged 100,000 Yemeni rials (about £320) a family, but let Saeed’s family travel despite having no money. The journey lasted nine hours.

Saeed is one of several thousand Yemenis who have fled into Djibouti in recent weeks. He is sheltering with other Yemeni nationals at the packed Markazi humanitarian site near the fishing town of Obock in the north-east of the country.
Pointing to his white T-shirt, the same one he wore while fleeing, he said: “I left everything behind.”

The renewed fighting in Yemen has created a dire humanitarian situation. More than 900 people have been killed, and at least 250,000 have been forced out of their homes since the beginning of August. The clashes exacerbated an existing crisis in the country, where the UN estimates that more than half the population needs humanitarian assistance.

“Ongoing fighting, insecurity and restrictions on movement are making it increasingly difficult to reach displaced communities and deliver assistance safely,” said Laila Al Amine, regional programmes director at the Prosper Global charity (formerly Mercy Corps), which is assisting displaced people in Taiz governorate, where more than 100,000 have sought refuge. “After more than a decade of conflict, families in Yemen should not have to keep running in search of safety.”

The governorate’s capital, Taiz, and Yemen’s south-western Red Sea coast, including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a strategic global trade position at the intersection of Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea – have all witnessed heavy fighting during the renewed conflict, as Houthi militia and the Yemeni forces battle for territory.
In recent weeks fighting has intensified around Taiz, the third-largest city in Yemen, as Houthis encircle it and take control of routes in and out of the city, raising fears of a siege.

On a recent sweltering day at the Markazi humanitarian site, families sat beside mounds of their belongings, including mattresses, jerrycans and buckets. Children played on a swing and women in burqas chatted in clusters.
A mile away from the humanitarian site, a few hundred Yemenis staggered towards it carrying aid packages from a government warehouse.

Inside a building at the site where she and her family are staying, Madinah Abdullah painfully recollected surviving airstrikes and gunfire in her home city of Mocha in September, then fleeing after Houthis took over from retreating government forces. “We were living on the frontline,” said the 43-year-old.

Abdullah said Houthis forcibly recruited boys and young men, or accused them of working with government forces. She was especially worried the group would take her 16-year-old son. “I was afraid Houthis would see my son,” she said.
They hid until an opportune moment presented itself, and they and their seven other family members took a fishing boat to Djibouti with about 40 other people.
“Life in Mocha was very good before the conflict, but Houthis disrupted everything,” said Abdullah, who used to work with an aid organisation.
In Markazi, Yemenis found a site that was already hosting refugees, including fellow nationals who arrived after the outbreak of the civil war in 2014.

As of 8 October, the number of new Yemeni arrivals had reached 3,807, according to Yemen’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims. Mahdi Osman, coordinator at the agency, said there was increasing pressure on shelter capacity, water supply, sanitation facilities, food assistance and healthcare services. “The main challenge lies in the gap between the rapid pace of arrivals and the resources available to receive newly arrived refugees and meet their essential needs,” he said.

“Djibouti continues to demonstrate solidarity with people forced to flee conflict, despite its limited resources. We call on the international community to stand alongside the government of Djibouti to ensure that every person arriving in the country has access to effective protection, shelter and essential services.”

Yemen’s civil war erupted in 2014 when Houthis took control of the country’s capital, Sana’a, and the government. In response, a coalition led by neighbouring Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates carried out a military campaign to reinstate the Yemeni government.

A ceasefire facilitated by the UN was established in 2022 and was mostly adhered to until July, when Houthis fired drones and missiles towards Saudi Arabia in response to what they said were Saudi airstrikes on the international airport in Sana’a aimed at preventing an Iranian plane carrying Yemenis from landing.

In early September Houthis launched a lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing key positions around the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, which had become an important route for Saudi oil exports because of disruptions in the strait of Hormuz caused by the US war against Iran.

Houthi militias have also launched attacks on Saudi airports, tankers and oil facilities. On 10 October, a missile attack by the rebel group on King Khalid International airport in the capital, Riyadh, killed 13 people. Experts fear the escalating conflict could draw additional countries into the crisis.
For many Yemenis who have fled to Djibouti, the recent displacement is yet another mark of the war on their lives.

Aisha Ismail still has a bullet in her leg from a shooting that happened at the onset of the civil war. She fled to Djibouti in September with her sister and their elderly father, who has a hearing impairment. “War, gunfire and bombing,” she said of the factors that had driven them to leave their home.

The 33-year-old added: “We just ran away because we have no men to protect us. My father is an old man and he is now 85 years old and we have no brother or uncle. Out of fear, we just ran away without taking anything. We left everything behind. All our belongings.”
From their home town of Dhubab, just north of the Bab al-Mandab strait, they trekked for miles to find a boat to Djibouti, and finally made the journey across with more than 100 other people.

Ismail used to sell potatoes to sustain herself, her father and her sister. She bemoans that although food is distributed at the site, it’s never enough. “The last time I ate something was yesterday,” she said one late morning.

Saeed is often occupied with volunteering at a water collection point, where he helps children and other vulnerable people draw water from a tap, “so that everyone has a fair opportunity to access water without confusion”.
Like those of many others at the site, his thoughts often return to his home in Yemen. “My hope,” he said, “is that the war will end so that I can return home with my family and live in peace”.

articles.title: Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’
articles.summary: Apparent attempt to hack Rade Bajić’s iPhone comes amid efforts to undermine landmark criminal case
body: A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates.
Related: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business

The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities.
Rade Bajić, the targeted prosecutor, said: “In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.”

Analysts at the Citizen Lab, a digital forensics laboratory, have not so far established who was behind the attack but the Serbian regime has previously been caught using spyware against its opponents.

News of the alleged hack follows the Guardian’s revelations last week that Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, personally ordered that a cherished site in Belgrade be stripped of its legal protection so it could be handed over for a $500m Trump hotel and tower. Vučić, one of the Balkans’ most influential nationalists, hosted the US president’s son Donald Jr – “dear Don”, as he calls him – and son-in-law Jared Kushner as he ingratiated himself with the Trumps.

At the weekend, Vučić responded to the Guardian’s revelations about his role in the scandal by confirming details of a previously secret meeting. He indicated he had done nothing wrong. “I fought for my people,” he said. “And that’s what I’ll continue to do in the future.”

Last year prosecutors brought a landmark indictment against senior members of Vučić’s regime, accusing them of abusing their office to unlawfully strip the General Staff building – a monument to Serbia’s recent difficult history – of its protected status. They face years in jail if convicted.

Kushner, who was leading the Trump Belgrade development, called off the plans after the charges were made public. Vučić vowed reprisals, denouncing the prosecutors, including Bajić, a member of the specialised organised-crime unit that brought the indictment.

Bajić has said he was taken off the case without explanation shortly before the indictment was published. He went on to address one of the rolling protests against the regime triggered by widespread corruption, telling demonstrators in February: “The law will be equal for all.”
In August, Bajić received a message from Apple saying it had “detected a targeted mercenary attack against your iPhone”.
Citizen Lab researchers, who have been analysing Bajić’s phone, said this was “a high confidence indicator that his device was likely targeted with mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus”.

Working with the Share Foundation, a Serbian rights group, they previously identified spyware attacks against anti-government protesters. In at least one case, the Citizen Lab analysts discovered Pegasus on a protester’s phone. “A zero-click infection with Pegasus spyware would not have been visible to the target, and would give the Pegasus attacker total access to the device,” they said of that discovery.

The Guardian’s Pegasus Project revealed how journalists, activists, politicians and others have been targeted by governments using the spyware. NSO Group, the Israel-based company that makes Pegasus, has been approached for comment.

Vučić, who stepped down late last month and called snap elections for 25 October, hoping to prolong his 12-year rule by switching from president to prime minister. He has been approached for comment, as has the prosecutors’ unit, which has said it may bring more charges in the General Staff building case.

Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner have denied they engaged in “pay to play” arrangements and said they were not involved in the Serbian authorities’ decision to strip the building of its protected status.

articles.title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukrainian president accuses Washington of ‘denial of reality’ in continuing row with Trump over apparent support for Moscow
body: Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.

Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian air force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at about 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.

“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.

“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Zelenskyy is grappling with recent US moves benefiting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin.

On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.

The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

Trump also told reporters on Monday that he would consider a trilateral meeting with Russia and China. He said: “We ‌would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation. If ‌President Xi wants to have it, I’d ​have it.”

For years, the US has warned Ukraine before Russia launched ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.

Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”

US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.

The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.

Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St Petersburg.

The Russian barrage on Sunday evening hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than 500,000 people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping centres, fuel stations and supermarkets, among other sites.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, and officials in the capital reported that a 21-year-old woman had been killed.

Later drone strikes on a public park in the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people, including young children. The regional governor, Oleg Synegubov, said on Telegram that three of the dead in the attack on Nova Vodolaha were children, including one in a pushchair. Seven children were among the 14 wounded. Police posted pictures showing damaged playground equipment.

Synegubov condemned “another terrorist act by the Russian Federation”, saying “the enemy strikes a recreational park in the middle of the day, knowing that there is no military infrastructure there at all”.

Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Zelenskyy on Monday to discuss the embattled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, according to a Vatican statement. He told the Ukrainian president that he had asked Putin for a humanitarian ceasefire during a call with the Russian leader on Friday.

Residents of Oleshky face a worsening humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food and medication, as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The Vatican said that Leo had expressed deep concern about conditions in the city and sought a ceasefire to permit aid deliveries and evacuations.
The call to Zelenskyy came two days after Leo, 71, was discharged from a hospital in Rome where he underwent a lung cancer operation on Tuesday.
The Kremlin said on Friday it had explained to Leo what it called “the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation”.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Can Andy Burnham beat Britain’s headphone dodgers?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister’s campaign against noisy passengers has struck a chord with commuters. Whether anyone hears him remains to be seen
body: Me again, back from the October school holiday (a week in glorious Wales, thanks for asking) and ready to hear your commuter woes. For our prime minister, it’s “one of the most annoying things on public transport”: maybe you’re trying to work, or read, or you’ve finally got your kid to sleep, when someone starts blasting sound from their phone at full volume.

As I sign off this First Edition en route from Glasgow to London (the things I’ve heard on this commute, against my will, I’ll save for another newsletter), I’m hoping everyone has been paying attention.

I’m struck by how few voices there have been suggesting Burnham should be concentrating on more important matters. It seems to me that other people’s noise, and other inconsiderate behaviour on public transport, has become shorthand for wider concerns about social cohesion, generational conflict and political fragmentation. Put simply, we are all making much more noise, and have become much worse at listening to what anyone else is actually saying. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to a bus driver, a transport expert and a cultural critic to find out more. That’s after the headlines.

France | The prime minister has said he has asked regional authorities to impose partial curfews in some cities after the government admitted police had “lost control” in several places during violent weekend protests around the country.
UK politics | Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.

Yemen | At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government forces in the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
Israel | Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine.
Reform | Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.

When Andy Burnham launched his crusade against unnecessary noise and antisocial behaviour on public transport with a chatty Instagram post recorded on a morning train into Manchester Piccadilly, my first thought was: “I bet he didn’t upload that on the dodgy onboard wifi.”

The prime minister’s sights were set on the phenomenon described as “loudcasting” or “headphone dodging” – but you don’t need a specialist term, because you know it when you hear the passenger next to you blasting Facebook slop on loudspeaker.

Alongside a nationwide campaign encouraging people to plug in their headphones and “share the carriage, not the noise,” Burnham announced new guidance to help local transport authorities introduce fines of up to £100 for nuisance behaviour like vaping, littering and playing loud music or videos on buses. Train operating companies already have powers to impose fines of up to £1,000 for antisocial behaviour.
If you’re grinding your molars at the thought, you’re not alone. A hefty majority of Britons, about 88% according to recent polling, consider it unacceptable to play music out loud on a train.
Who will actually enforce the rules?

It’s still unclear how these new rules would be enforced. Government officials have reassured bus drivers that they won’t be expected to police passengers themselves. That job will fall on transport safety officers or police officers.

Mark, a bus driver in central London, tells me he and his colleagues simply don’t have the capacity to help. He spends his working life in the glass cabinet at the front of the vehicle. He can’t hear every noise or spot every puff of vape smoke on the top deck, and, as well as navigating the city traffic, he already has other things to focus on, such as fare-dodging.

Mark’s route has become noisier in recent years, though he’s keen not to point out “it’s an all-ages” issue, and not to lay the blame solely with younger passengers. He doubts whether Burnham can isolate the problem to public transport. “It’s a whole society thing: being kinder and more aware of their environment.”
“It’s not workable without resources,” he says. “I don’t really see how it would be enforceable: you can’t have someone on every bus and train.”
Here lies the difficulty: fines for nuisance noise on trains are already vanishingly rare, with offenders able to shut up or leave the carriage before enforcement arrives.

The number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers has fallen by more than 10% over the past two years. The people left to challenge the noisy doom-scroller are, therefore, you and me. Transport for London, for example, has done some great work on bystander intervention, suggesting straightforward ways to interrupt bad behaviour without putting yourself in danger, but many of us would think twice about confronting a stranger in the confines of a moving vehicle.
Is this a crackdown on bad behaviour, or a distraction from worse problems?

Not everyone is impressed by the scale of the response. Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite – a woman resolutely resistant to hoping, again – described the new policy as “well-meaning but wholly inadequate” to tackle the “avalanche of escalating abuse” faced by the transport workers she represents.

“There has been a massive escalation in reported assaults on public transport across the country,” says our transport correspondent Gwyn Topham, who reported earlier this month on the growing number of verbal and physical assaults faced by transport workers and passengers. In my previous incarnation as Scotland correspondent, I wrote about bus driver Keith Rollinson, who died at Elgin bus station after a violent assault by a teenage passenger.

Thoughtlessly broadcasting your TikTok scrolling is at the other end of the spectrum, but there’s an argument that antisocial behaviour exists on a continuum, and that a “nip it in the bud” approach might prevent more serious problems from escalating. Zero tolerance policing of course has a mixed record – and if you detect Tony Blair vibes here, so do I. Dropping a grand for loudcasting your tunes has more than a whiff of New Labour’s respect agenda and the classist asbo culture it ushered in, which singularly failed to tackle antisocial behaviour at its roots.

Still, there’s much to be said for elevating the issue from shared eye-rolls to official tannoy announcements. This is a policy that is going to appeal hugely to commuters, Gywn predicts, and when we are speaking he points out that the article about the campaign launch has been most-read across the Guardian website throughout the morning. “What he’s done well is to acknowledge an everyday irritation, that doesn’t cost a lot of money to fix, but can hopefully alter public behaviour.”
Can telling people to behave better work?

Gentle nudges towards more respectful behaviour, rather than sledgehammer fines, have made a difference historically, writer Dan Hancox tells me. His latest book, Multitudes, is about crowd behaviour, and recalls “a real moral panic” in the early 2010s over teenagers playing tinny MP3s aloud from basic mobile phones.

Dan could see why people found this irritating, but defended it at the time: “It was a rare example of sharing of music as a social adhesive, at a moment when David Cameron was introducing austerity and the spaces in which young people could gather together were being shut down.”
Crucially, within a couple of years the behaviour had died down again, as often happens after the initial buzz around new technology and the social pressure points they create.

But this phenomenon of people playing video out loud on their phones has got noticeably worse in the last couple of years, he believes, and, as I match Dan’s anecdotal experience with my own, it’s not all about the young ones this time. Indeed, younger travellers seem more likely to rely on noise-cancelling headphones – which some audiologists have raised concerns over potential links to auditory processing problems.

So why are otherwise apparently mature adults broadcasting their content and calls on the bus? The notion that people have “forgotten how to behave” since the Covid lockdown is one that Dan refutes. “It feels like an easy answer for something that is much more complex,” he says. “But it didn’t go on for that long, and the really remarkable thing about human beings is how quickly and elastically they bounce back to their previous sets of behaviours.”
The more boring answer, he suggests from his own research, is that as 5G makes watching videos easier to do wherever we are – people are simply seizing that opportunity.

But crowd psychology tells us that other people’s propensity to broadcast noise has a minimal effect on our own behaviour. “People’s pre-existing values and social mores are incredibly robust and are unlikely to change based on the behaviour of a complete stranger,” says Dan. And this makes it much more susceptible to the kind of nudge messaging over the train tannoy that Burnham is proposing.

In my own experience of antisocial behaviour on public transport, it seems that two things can be true at once: there’s a growing anxiety that this indicates an unravelling of the social contract, and in the main our interactions with fellow passengers often reassure us this is not, in fact, the case.

It’s possible that anxiety about strangers and the malign influence of the crowd arises at moments of wider pressures, says Dan. “When people are worried about paying the rent or feeding their families, as wars in the wider world rock our sense of stability and faith in human beings, our suspicion of the random person on the bus grows.

“But my day-to-day experience of life in a big and supposedly alienating city like London tells me people want this kind of spontaneous connection more than ever, and it’s a joy when it happens. Even if it’s just a few warm words exchanged with a stranger at the bus stop, on the train or in the shops – this is what it means to live in a society.”
Next week, the chancellor, John Healey, will deliver his first budget. We want to hear what you think the chancellor should do, so email us at first.edition@theguardian.com.

Thanks to Jessica Murray’s excellent preview, I’ll be heading to the Senate House Library’s new exhibition, which charts the history of housing and poverty in London over the past 200 years – and reveals how much (and how little) has changed. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

I regularly pace around my neighbourhood (or living room) before bed if I’m yet to hit my 10,000 daily steps. After Kate Lloyd investigated whether this target was arbitrary, I fear I’ll no longer bother. Michael

“Some scientists say that we are living through the largest loss of life since the time of the dinosaurs”: Patrick Greenfield’s piece about quite how much is at stake at the Cop17 biodiversity summit is a sobering and important read. Lucinda

Come Dine With Me fans will appreciate this week’s How we made column on the C4 show. Not sure I’ve seen the episode mentioned where a pet snake crapped all over a dining table, but host-puts-whole-whisk in mouth is a classic. Michael

If you need an easy DIY Halloween costume this year, Guardian writers and readers have got you. Top suggestions include dressing up as a Freudian slip (by wearing a slip dress with “ego”, “id” and “preconscious” written across it) and donning an LED face mask without the light turned on – genuinely chilling. Lucinda
Football | James Maddison scored an excellent first goal, before Omar Marmoush and Ben Davies wrapped up the scoring as Spurs beat a stubborn Coventry 3-1.

Gymnastics | The judge who sentenced the former USA Gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar to up to 175 years in jail in 2018 for the sexual abuse of more than 250 women and girls has condemned the lack of meaningful change in the decade since Nassar’s crimes were exposed.
Sport | Australian Scott Boland quick ended the day with four wickets against South Africa who finished on 97-5 on the second day of the test match.

“Burnham orders radical rethink of options to fix Thames Water”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times leads with “No increase to capital gains tax in the budget”, the Mail writes “Kemi: Budget could be even worse than Reeves bloodbath”, the Telegraph has “Labour cuts £2bn from Army from front line”, and the i Paper runs with “Two-child cap on childcare benefits will be lifted by April”.

The FT leads on “Challenges facing Macron deepen after street clashes reignite French debt rout”, and Metro has “The French correction”. The Express splashes on “NHS is ‘simply not ready’ for another winter crisis”, and the Sun on an RAF crash probe writes “Air heads”.
France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests

Last weekend there were mass protests across France, with more than half a million people estimated to have been involved. The unrest included rioting, looting and violent clashes with outnumbered police in cities including Paris, Marseille and Limoges. The interior minister conceded that police ‘lost control’ in some cities, while President Emmanuel Macron demanded a full security review. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Europe correspondent, Jon Henley.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

In 2022, bird flu wiped out the colony of sandwich terns nesting at Pagham harbour, West Sussex. But their numbers have since bounced back to 756 breeding pairs – and populations of other birds such as ringed plovers and oystercatchers have also increased along the same coastline.

The turnaround is thanks to conservation efforts by RSPB staff and volunteers, which have included removing certain vegetation to make space for shorebirds to nest, and erecting special fencing to keep out predators such as foxes.

The RSPB’s Wez Smith said: “It’s taken several years of dedicated conservation action, but the situation began to ‘tern’ around last year, and the site is now thriving with record breaking populations using it.”
